q: In an NFA, δ(q, a) is…
options: a set of states, which may be empty
always a non-empty set of states
a state together with a stack symbol
explain: δ : Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → 𝒫(Q). A move can lead to several states, one state, or none (that branch dies).

q: An NFA accepts a string w when…
options: at least one way of reading w ends in a final state
every way of reading w ends in a final state
exactly one way of reading w ends in a final state
the last branch it tries ends in a final state
explain: Nondeterministic acceptance is existential: one successful path is enough. Dead or rejecting branches do not matter.

q: NFAs can recognise some languages that no DFA can recognise.
explain: False. The subset construction converts every NFA into a DFA for the same language, so both recognise exactly the regular languages.

q: The subset construction is applied to an NFA with n states. The resulting DFA has at most…
explain: Each DFA state is a subset of the n NFA states, and there are 2ⁿ subsets, including ∅. In practice you build only the reachable ones.

q: An ε-NFA has the ε-moves q₀ → q₁ and q₁ → q₂, and no other ε-moves. What is ECLOSE(q₀)?
explain: The ε-closure contains q₀ itself, plus everything reachable by ε-moves alone: q₁, and then q₂ from q₁.

q: Same ε-NFA: q₀ —ε→ q₁ —ε→ q₂, δ(q₂, a) = {q₂, q₃}, and F = {q₃}. What is the length of the shortest accepted string?
explain: ECLOSE(q₀) = {q₀, q₁, q₂} does not contain q₃, so ε is rejected. On 'a', q₂ moves to {q₂, q₃}, which contains the final state. So 'a', of length 1, is the shortest.

q: What language over {0, 1} does this NFA accept?
dot: digraph { node [shape=circle]; start [shape=none, label=""]; q2 [shape=doublecircle]; start -> q0; q0 -> q0 [label="0, 1"]; q0 -> q1 [label="1"]; q1 -> q2 [label="0, 1"]; }
explain: The NFA guesses the 1 that is followed by exactly one more symbol. q₂ has no outgoing moves, so the input must end right there. The 1 is therefore second from the end.

q: Using the same NFA (q₀ loops on 0, 1; q₀ —1→ q₁; q₁ —0, 1→ q₂, final), which strings are accepted?
explain: 10 and 110 have 1 as their second-to-last symbol. 01 has 0 there, and 1 is too short to have a second-to-last symbol.

q: In the subset construction, when is a DFA state S (a set of NFA states) final?
options: When S contains at least one NFA final state
When every state in S is final
When S contains the NFA start state
When S is the largest reachable set
explain: The DFA is in S when the NFA could be in any state of S. One accepting possibility is enough for the NFA to accept.

q: Over {0, 1}, an NFA with 4 states accepts the strings whose third symbol from the end is 1. What is the smallest DFA for this language?
explain: A DFA must remember the last three symbols, because any two different 3-symbol suffixes can be told apart by some continuation. That needs 2³ = 8 states: the exponential blow-up really happens.
